chunks: al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad — both together — from al-Washa', from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Whoever bequeaths a third has indeed harmed the inheritors; and the bequest of a fifth and a quarter is better than the bequest of a third; and whoever bequeaths a third has not held anything back.

key_terms.الثلث: al-Thuluth — one-third; the maximum legally permissible bequest under Islamic law
key_terms.الخمس: al-Khums — one-fifth; recommended as a more moderate bequest
key_terms.الربع: al-Rub' — one-quarter; also recommended as a more balanced bequest
key_terms.الورثة: al-Waratha — the inheritors/heirs who receive fixed Quranic shares (fara'id)
key_terms.الوصية: Wasiyyah — the testamentary bequest, a legal instrument in Islamic inheritance law allowing up to one-third of the estate to be directed outside the Quranic shares

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about bequeathing one-third of one's estate to non-heirs?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) delivers a legal ruling discouraging the maximum permitted bequest of one-third of an estate, teaching that bequeathing a fifth or quarter is more virtuous and less harmful to the heirs. Islamic law (following Quran 2:180 and 4:11) permits a person to bequeath up to one-third of their estate to non-heirs; while this maximum is legally allowed, the Imam indicates it is ethically preferable to leave a larger share for one's family by bequeathing less. The phrase 'has not held anything back' (فَلَمْ يَتْرُكْ) implies the person has been excessively generous to the detriment of their family.
